message:
QUESTION:
Did the 1 June move to a new content delivery network (CDN) improve the site's conversion rate, and what is a faster site worth?

DATA:
An online retailer migrated its website to a new content delivery network (CDN) on 1 June. Two weeks before (18-31 May) vs two weeks after (1-14 June):

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June |
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 |
| Median page load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s |
| 95th-percentile page load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% |

Conversion = orders / sessions. Page load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views.

Same two calendar periods last year, when there were no site or infrastructure changes: conversion 2.4% (18-31 May) and 2.6% (1-14 June).

The retailer's conversion rate rises every year in early June when the summer ranges launch. This year the summer ranges again launched on 1 June. No other site changes were made between 18 May and 14 June.

KNOWN FLAWS:
F1. [calculation] The reduction is (7.5 − 4.8) / 7.5 = 36%. 56% comes from dividing the 2.7 s fall by the new value (4.8). The draft's claim that the slowest experiences 'improved even more' than the median (34%) is barely true at 36%. CORRECTION: 95th percentile fell by 36%, similar to the median's 34%.
F2. [misreport] The data show bounce rate fell from 48% to 44%. CORRECTION: A 4-point (8% relative) fall in bounce rate.
F3. [method] Ignores the seasonal baseline: the same calendar periods last year, with no site changes, show the same 0.2-point rise (2.4% to 2.6%) from the summer range launch, which happened again on 1 June. CORRECTION: Year-over-year difference-in-differences: (2.70 − 2.50) − (2.6 − 2.4) = 0.0 points. There is no detectable conversion effect of the CDN.
F4. [inference] Derives a linear causal 'value per second' from one confounded before/after comparison and extrapolates it beyond the observed range. CORRECTION: The data support no value-per-second estimate (the seasonally adjusted effect is about zero). A randomised latency experiment would be needed.

EXTENSIONS:
- Run a statistical check on the raw conversion change (2.50% vs 2.70%, z of about 4) and contrast it with the seasonally adjusted comparison, showing that a highly significant before/after change can be entirely seasonal.
- Check whether the sessions increase (+5%) is also seasonal, using last year's session counts for the same periods, which the analyst should request.
- Segment by device or connection type: speed gains typically matter most on mobile and slow connections, so an effect masked in the aggregate could appear there (data would be needed).

FINAL VERSION:
# Receipt

**Verdict.** The reviewer judges the analysis sound. The figures are correct, the main conclusion is right (the conversion rise matches last year's seasonal rise), and declining to give a per-second value is correct. Nothing about the conclusions would change.

**Arithmetic check.** The reviewer re-derived every figure and found them correct. I re-checked them too and agree, with one small correction to the review's own working. The "8.0%" seasonal lift for this year is 0.2 ÷ 2.5 (the May baseline). It is not 0.2 ÷ 2.7 as the review's table shows, which would give 7.4%. The analysis figure is right; only the review's check line is mis-stated. Nothing in the analysis needs to change for this.

**Issue 1: last year's rates are rounded.** Last year's 2.4% and 2.6% are given to one decimal place, so each could be off by up to ±0.05 points. Last year's lift could therefore be anywhere from 0.1 to 0.3 points. That alone puts the CDN estimate anywhere from about −0.1 to +0.1 points, before any sampling error. *Change:* say this explicitly in the precision section. Soften "exactly the same amount" to "the same amount, to the precision available." Add the unrounded figures and last year's session counts to the data request.

**Issue 2: "roughly doubles that uncertainty" overstates it.** With similar traffic last year, comparing the two years doubles the variance, not the interval. The 95% interval widens by about √2, from ±0.10 to about ±0.14 points. *Change:* reword to "widens the interval to roughly ±0.15 points or more." Note that this can't be pinned down without last year's session counts.

**Suggestion: speed caveat.** New summer ranges change page content and image weight, which could move load times either way. *Change:* soften "the summer launch would not be expected to make pages load faster" to acknowledge this, while keeping the conclusion that the CDN is the likely cause.

**Suggestion: separate the corrections list.** The "Corrections to the draft" list refers to a document readers may not have. *Change:* take it out of the main analysis and keep it as a separate note for the draft's author.

**Suggestion: next step 1.** Deliberately slowing pages for some customers costs revenue. *Change:* lead with the alternative design (testing a speed improvement on a random share of traffic), and flag the cost of the slow-down design.

**Suggestion: next step 4.** *Change:* add last year's unrounded conversion rates and session counts to the data pull.

---

# CDN migration: performance and conversion impact

## Summary

The new CDN made the site substantially faster. Median page load time fell by about a third, and the slowest page loads improved by a similar proportion.

The rise in conversion over the same period cannot be credited to the CDN. Conversion rose by 0.2 points, from 2.50% to 2.70%. Over the same calendar weeks last year it also rose by 0.2 points (2.4% to 2.6%), when nothing on the site changed. In both years the summer ranges launched on 1 June. Once that seasonal lift is allowed for, the best estimate of the CDN's effect on conversion is about zero. The estimate is imprecise, though, and a moderate effect in either direction cannot be ruled out.

These data therefore cannot tell us what a faster site is worth. We need a controlled test to answer that.

## Speed

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median load time | 3.2 s | 2.1 s | −1.1 s (−34%) |
| 95th-percentile load time | 7.5 s | 4.8 s | −2.7 s (−36%) |

Load times come from real-user monitoring across all page views. They reflect what customers experienced on their own devices and connections. In relative terms, the slowest page loads improved slightly more than the typical one. Half of page loads now complete within 2.1 seconds, and 95% within 4.8 seconds.

The improvement is large, and its timing matches the migration. The summer launch did change page content and image weight, which could move load times either way. However, a content change is unlikely to cut load times by a third at both the median and the 95th percentile. Higher seasonal traffic would, if anything, tend to slow the site. The CDN is very likely the main cause of the speed gain.

## Engagement and volume

| Metric | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 200,000 | 210,000 | +5% |
| Orders | 5,000 | 5,670 | +13% |
| Orders per day | ~357 | ~405 | +13% |
| Bounce rate | 48% | 44% | −4 points (−8% relative) |

Bounce rate is the share of sessions that view only one page. A faster site could explain the fall in bounce rate. So could the summer launch, since new ranges give visitors more reasons to browse. We do not have last year's bounce rate for the same weeks, so we cannot separate the two causes.

## Conversion

| | 18-31 May | 1-14 June | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| This year (new CDN from 1 June) | 2.50% | 2.70% | +0.20 points |
| Last year (no site changes) | 2.4% | 2.6% | +0.2 points |
| **Difference (estimated CDN effect)** | | | **≈ 0 points** |

In relative terms the seasonal lift was about 8% in both years: 8.3% last year (0.2 ÷ 2.4) and 8.0% this year (0.2 ÷ 2.5). The summer range launch alone is enough to explain all of this year's increase.

The CDN was the only *site* change in the period, but it was not the only change. The summer launch happened on the same day, and a simple before/after comparison cannot separate the two.

**Precision.** The estimate of about zero is uncertain, for four reasons:

- **Sampling error this year.** Two weeks of data per period is short. Treating sessions as independent, the 95% interval on this year's 0.2-point rise is about ±0.1 points.
- **Sampling error in the comparison.** Comparing against last year adds last year's sampling error. If last year had similar traffic, the interval on the CDN effect widens to roughly ±0.15 points or more. The exact figure needs last year's session counts.
- **Rounding.** Last year's rates are given to one decimal place, so last year's lift could be anywhere from about 0.1 to 0.3 points. Rounding alone leaves the CDN effect anywhere from about −0.1 to +0.1 points.
- **Other variation.** Day-to-day swings add more uncertainty. A single year is also a weak guide to the normal seasonal lift, because the strength of the summer launch varies from year to year.

Taken together, a CDN effect of a couple of tenths of a point in either direction cannot be excluded. That is up to roughly ±10% of conversion, or several hundred orders a fortnight. The honest conclusion is that there is **no detectable conversion effect**. That is not the same as proof that there is no effect.

## What is a second worth?

These data do not support a per-second figure, for three reasons:

1. **The observed 0.2 points is seasonal.** After removing the seasonal lift, the change attributable to speed is about zero, with wide uncertainty. Dividing that by 1.1 seconds gives a number that is neither credible nor useful.
2. **One before/after pair cannot reveal a rate.** We have a single change in speed and a single change in conversion. We cannot tell whether the relationship is linear or shows diminishing returns. Going from 3.2 s to 2.1 s may matter quite differently from going from 2.1 s to 1.1 s.
3. **The choice of speed metric is arbitrary.** The median improved by 1.1 seconds and the 95th percentile by 2.7 seconds. Dividing by one or the other gives different "per-second" values from the same data.

## Next steps

1. **Run a controlled test to measure the value of speed.** The preferred design is to roll out a specific speed improvement to a random share of traffic and compare conversion with the rest. An alternative is to add a small, controlled delay for a random share of traffic. That design gives a cleaner reading on the value of speed, but it has a direct revenue cost while it runs, and stakeholders should agree to that in advance. Either design removes seasonality and gives a defensible conversion effect per second.
2. **Use the real-user monitoring data from the post-migration period.** Compare conversion across sessions or segments with different load times, such as device type, region and connection type. Control for traffic source and product category. Also compare segments where the CDN cut load times most with those where it changed little. This is weaker evidence than a test but quicker to produce.
3. **Do not use a points-per-second figure in business cases** until step 1 or step 2 produces one.
4. **Pull last year's full data for the same weeks.** This means unrounded conversion rates, session and order counts, and bounce rate. That data will tighten the seasonal comparison and allow engagement to be adjusted for seasonality in the same way as conversion. Separately, keep monitoring load times weekly through the summer to confirm that the speed gains hold as traffic grows.
5. **Value the CDN on its other merits as well.** These include hosting and bandwidth costs, reliability, and search ranking. None of them depends on a measurable conversion lift.

## Conclusion

The CDN migration made the site about a third faster, at both the median and the 95th percentile. Conversion rose by 0.2 points, but it rose by the same amount, to the precision available, at the same point last year because of the summer range launch. There is no evidence yet that the faster site improved conversion. The data are too imprecise to rule out a moderate effect either way. The value of a second of load time needs to be measured with a controlled test; it cannot be inferred from this before/after comparison.

---

## Note for the draft's author (separate from the analysis)

These are the corrections made to the earlier draft:

- **95th-percentile reduction:** 36%, not 56%.
- **Bounce rate:** fell from 48% to 44%, not to 32%. That is a 4-point fall (8% relative), not a fall "by a third".
- **Attribution:** the draft credited the conversion rise to the CDN. Last year's matching seasonal rise shows that this isn't supported.
- **Dropped figures:** the "420 extra orders a fortnight" and "0.18 points per second" have been removed, because both rest on that attribution.
- **1.1-second target:** removed, because it relied on extrapolating a straight line from a single before/after pair.
